title: Scale Up, Scale Out Challenges Amplified For Clusters
gist: A roundtable of Arm, Cadence, Expedera, Siemens EDA, Synopsys, and Axiomise engineers argues power, not GPU availability, is now the binding constraint on AI compute clusters, and that the industry-wide shift from training to inference (expected to be over 80% of AI workloads) is elevating the CPU to a central orchestration role alongside GPUs, while scale-up and scale-out are fundamentally different latency/bandwidth engineering problems, not the same problem at different sizes.

themes.theme: Power, not GPU supply, is now the binding constraint

insights.claim: Power has replaced GPU availability as the primary bottleneck constraining AI cluster scaling, and data center customers increasingly cannot run all their GPUs at full power simultaneously due to insufficient power capacity.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: A structural shift in the binding constraint from chip supply to power infrastructure redirects investor attention from GPU-allocation plays toward power-delivery, grid capacity, and power-aware scheduling software as the next scarce resource in the AI buildout.
insights.quote: Power is becoming the bottleneck now. Initially, it was the GPU availability and the like, but now it is coming down to power.

insights.claim: Data center operators are running GPUs at partial power (e.g., roughly 50%) because the performance loss is disproportionately smaller than the power savings, so intelligent cluster middleware software that identifies the right power/performance operating point can materially improve power-per-token economics versus simply running all applications at max power.
insights.speaker: Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Establishes 'power per token' as an emerging efficiency metric investors should track for AI infrastructure operators, and signals a software opportunity (cluster middleware for power/performance tuning) that sits above the hardware layer.
insights.quote: Maybe you can run it at 50%, but it doesn’t double the time it takes, and you get better power per performance. They talk about power per token.
insights.locator: Brunner on running GPUs at partial power

insights.claim: AI-driven automation of power/performance steering (monitoring workload history, running experiments, dynamically assigning workloads to GPUs with the best-fit power/performance profile) is an area Nvidia is heavily investing in, though today it largely still requires manual human experimentation.
insights.speaker: Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Confirms Nvidia is building automated power-control capability into its cluster software stack, a named competitive signal for infrastructure software vendors evaluating where Nvidia is extending its platform moat beyond silicon.
insights.quote: it’s something Nvidia is really big on: power control. You can even identify different power performance profiles that you see per individual GPUs in a given cluster, so being able to steer workloads to specific machines that have different performance profiles is a feasible thing. I think AI will help really enable some of that automation. Right now, a human can do it with the tools that we have.
insights.locator: Brunner on Nvidia and power control automation

insights.claim: Clusters do not automatically solve the power problem and can actually magnify it if the architecture forces excessive data movement; the right efficiency metric is useful work per joule across the full hierarchy (performance-per-watt), not raw power draw.
insights.speaker: Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a naive 'more clustering = more efficiency' narrative — investors evaluating cluster infrastructure vendors should ask specifically about performance-per-watt/useful-work-per-joule metrics rather than raw compute or power specs, since poor architecture can make clustering a net power negative.
insights.quote: Clusters don’t solve the power problem by themselves. They can actually magnify it if the architecture causes too much data movement.
insights.locator: Emmer on clusters and power per joule

insights.claim: Inference is expected to be over 80% of AI workloads going forward as models mature and move from training/deployment into steady-state serving, marking a structural shift in what kind of compute infrastructure is needed.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: An explicit, quantified forecast (80%+ inference share) that investors can use to reweight AI infrastructure exposure away from training-optimized GPU clusters and toward inference-optimized architectures (CPU-GPU orchestration, low-latency serving infrastructure).
insights.quote: is going to be +80% of the AI workloads going forward, as the models are getting more measured

insights.claim: As AI shifts from training to inference, agentic workloads (e.g., booking flights or Uber rides, doing research) run more efficiently on CPUs than GPUs because they are not matrix-multiplication-heavy, causing a close orchestration between CPU and GPU where CPUs absorb more of the workload at lower power while GPUs handle the accelerator-required reasoning portions.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: The CPU's rising centrality in agentic inference workloads is a specific, actionable thesis for CPU IP/design vendors (Arm) positioning against a GPU-centric AI infrastructure narrative — supports Arm's server/data-center CPU growth story as inference scales.
insights.quote: The CPU has started taking a very central role in terms of how these workloads are being served, especially as the shift is happening from training to inference.

insights.claim: Nvidia's Grace Hopper and Vera Rubin platforms exemplify the industry move toward tightly coupled CPU-GPU systems, and this paradigm is expected to require multiple companies collaborating on equivalent systems since no single company can build every layer alone.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: Names specific reference platforms (Grace Hopper, Vera Rubin) as the template the rest of the industry is racing to replicate — a competitive-landscape signal for evaluating which CPU/GPU/interconnect vendors are positioned to supply the 'equivalent system' ecosystem Bhattacharjee describes.
insights.quote: A good example is what Nvidia has done with Grace Hopper or Vera Rubin. There are a lot of innovations happening to create an equivalent system to scale this across, because you can’t rely on one company to do everything.

insights.claim: Training workloads behave like overnight batch jobs that can run at lower power during off-peak hours, whereas inference is a real-time, latency-sensitive workload typically run at consistently higher power, which changes how operators should schedule and price power consumption across workload types.
insights.speaker: Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete operational lever (time-shifting training to off-peak, low-power hours vs. always-on high-power inference) that data center operators can use to manage energy costs — relevant for evaluating power-aware scheduling software and utility demand-response deals tied to AI data centers.
insights.quote: The training workload is more like a batch workload. Let’s say you’ve got eight hours. You submit it at night because it needs to be done when you get into work the next day. We can run at lower power over the evening, whereas we’re maybe always running inference at higher power.
insights.locator: Brunner on training vs inference power scheduling

themes.theme: Memory hierarchy and KV cache innovation

insights.claim: In a typical CPU-GPU server sweet spot of two CPUs connected to eight GPUs, the CPU's memory hierarchy runs from per-core L2 cache (roughly 1-2 MB, nanosecond access) to shared L3 cache (roughly 1-2 MB per core, aggregating to over 100 MB across a 128-core CPU) to DDR main memory (gigabyte range, millisecond access) — each tier trading capacity for speed.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete quantitative map of the CPU memory hierarchy (capacity and latency at each tier) that underpins why memory bandwidth/latency innovation (not just raw compute) is a critical bottleneck and investment area in AI cluster design.
insights.quote: If there are 128 cores, you have 128 megabytes of cache. It’s still small. We’re still talking about megabytes, but it’s some of the fastest access that the cores have now.

insights.claim: Nvidia's NVLink allows faster-than-PCIe traffic between CPU and GPU, but has physical limits, so the industry is pursuing AMBA CHI as an open standard to let different CPUs and accelerators from different vendors achieve comparable interconnect speed-ups without depending on a single vendor's proprietary link.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: Signals an industry-wide effort (AMBA CHI) to reduce dependency on Nvidia's proprietary NVLink for CPU-accelerator interconnect — relevant for assessing whether Nvidia's interconnect moat faces credible open-standard competition over the medium term.
insights.quote: Nvidia has done a good job in coming up with NVLink, which allows it to push traffic at a much faster cadence over the physical link. There’s a physical limit, of course. It’s done with the PCIe connection, and that has some limits, but they are doing interesting stuff using AMBA CHI, which is an open standard to move the traffic.
insights.locator: Bhattacharjee on NVLink and AMBA CHI

insights.claim: For agentic AI workflows and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models handing tasks between multiple models, an active innovation area is keeping KV cache context in larger (cheaper, slower) memory when an agent is inactive, then pushing it back into fast, expensive accelerator memory (HBM) when the agent becomes active again.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm
insights.so_what: Identifies KV cache tiering/offload as a concrete, near-term software innovation area for agentic and MoE deployments — an efficiency lever that reduces reliance on scarce, expensive HBM capacity, relevant for memory-management software vendors and HBM suppliers alike.
insights.quote: Can you now keep some of these contexts, which are called KV cache, in the larger memory when the agent is not active, and then push them back to the accelerator memory when it’s active?

themes.theme: Networking and interconnect at cluster scale

insights.claim: A cluster's overall speed is limited by its slowest network switch, and inference workloads generate far more unpredictable, latency-sensitive traffic than training workloads because each query-response cycle involves someone actively waiting, unlike training's more tolerant batch patterns.
insights.speaker: Sumit Vishwakarma, director of strategic marketing at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Names networking/switch latency as 'the biggest bottleneck' explicitly — a clear investment signal toward interconnect, switch fabric, and low-latency networking vendors as inference-heavy traffic patterns scale, over pure compute silicon.
insights.quote: The architect needs to think about the cluster as one unit and not just design the silicon for that specific package, so networking is the biggest bottleneck. You are as fast as your slowest network switch.

insights.claim: Chips have evolved from single-die packages to multi-die and 3D-IC designs, adding new latency at every interconnect layer — die-to-die links (UCIe), and node-to-node links (Ethernet, UALink) — such that end-to-end latency now compounds across chip, package, and network boundaries.
insights.speaker: Sumit Vishwakarma, director of strategic marketing at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Maps the full latency stack across die-to-die (UCIe), rack-level (Ethernet/UALink) interconnect standards — useful for evaluating which interconnect-standard vendors and IP licensors are positioned across each layer of the AI cluster latency chain.
insights.quote: We are looking at this problem of die-to-die communication, where we have the UCIe kind of IPs for the fast data communication, all the way to Ethernet and UALink for cross communication between the nodes.
insights.locator: Vishwakarma on die-to-die and node interconnects

insights.claim: HPE's Dragonfly network topology was developed specifically to solve the problem of connecting hundreds of server racks (where no single switch has enough ports) without creating bottlenecks, after earlier hierarchical rack-trunking approaches caused jobs split across two racks to saturate connections and stall.
insights.speaker: Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: A concrete named example (HPE Dragonfly) of network topology innovation solving a real scale-out bottleneck — relevant for evaluating networking topology/switch vendors (HPE, Nvidia/Mellanox InfiniBand) competing to solve rack-to-rack scale-out interconnect at hyperscale.
insights.quote: Well, let’s say you have 500 racks. There isn’t a 500-port switch. How do you put all the racks together so you don’t incorporate bottlenecks? HPE has a strategy called Dragonfly Network Topology

themes.theme: Scale-up vs. scale-out are different engineering problems

insights.claim: The biggest mistake in cluster design is treating scale-up and scale-out as the same problem at different sizes: scale-up is about preserving locality and reducing serialization/deserialization overhead inside a package, while scale-out is about minimizing synchronization penalties and containing traffic amplification across racks, where the system must become far more selective about which traffic is truly latency-critical.
insights.speaker: Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence
insights.so_what: A clear framework investors can use to evaluate cluster-architecture vendors: solutions optimized for scale-up locality (in-package bandwidth) are not automatically transferable to scale-out synchronization problems, so due diligence on AI infrastructure vendors should ask which regime their product actually addresses.
insights.quote: The biggest mistake is to think that scale-up and scale-out are just the same problem at different sizes. They’re different latency and bandwidth regimes.

insights.claim: At cluster scale, overall performance is often determined less by peak compute capability and more by where data is forced to travel, making architectural efficiency a function of keeping weights, activations, KV cache, metadata, and control traffic local and exporting only what absolutely must move.
insights.speaker: Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence
insights.so_what: Reinforces that peak FLOPS/TOPS specs are an incomplete predictor of real cluster performance — data-locality-aware architecture is the differentiator, a useful diligence lens for evaluating AI accelerator and system vendors beyond headline compute benchmarks.
insights.quote: At the cluster scale, performance is often determined less by peak compute and more by where the data is forced to travel.
insights.locator: Emmer on data locality determining performance

insights.claim: Moving from a single server to a cluster fundamentally changes the correctness problem: a server is one tightly coupled failure domain, but a cluster consists of many independent components that can fail, restart, or become unreachable while the overall service keeps running, requiring architects to design in terms of protocols, distributed state, and recovery semantics rather than only local functional behavior.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise
insights.so_what: Frames verification/correctness itself as a distinct, harder discipline at cluster scale — relevant for evaluating formal verification vendors (Axiomise) whose addressable market expands as chip architects must now verify distributed-system-level correctness, not just single-chip functional behavior.
insights.quote: A server is one tightly coupled failure domain, while a cluster consists of many independent components that can fail, restart, or become unreachable while the overall service continues running.
